headline: Peconic settles into its August rhythm — porgies thick at Shelter Island, bass sliding into a night bite
subhead: Warm, calm water has the bay running on its usual late-summer clock, with porgies stacked on the reefs and stripers waiting for dark and moving current to feed.
body_markdown:
Every August the Peconic settles into the same pattern, and this year is no exception. The bay warms faster than the Sound every spring, and by now, deep into summer, it's holding that heat like a bathtub — calm, clear, and stable. That stability is exactly why the porgy fishing around Shelter Island has been as good as I've seen it in a few seasons, and why the fluke bite, while not blowing anyone's socks off, has been steady enough in the channels to keep rods bent.

Start with the porgies, because right now that's the most reliable thing going. Anchor up in Shelter Island Sound off the North Ferry crossing, or work the drop-offs near Jessup's Neck on the Noyack side, and you'll find them stacked in 15 to 25 feet of water over shell and mixed bottom. Standard hi-lo rigs with size 4 or 6 hooks, tipped with clam or squid strips, are doing the job — no need to get fancy. The bite has been best on the last two hours of the incoming tide into the top of high water, when the current slows enough for the porgies to really commit to the bait instead of just picking at it. Some of the fish coming over the rail are pushing into the 2-pound class, which for this bay is a genuinely good porgy. If you're teaching a kid to fish or just want a bucket of dinner, this is your week.

Fluke are a little more of a grind, but they're there if you work the right water. The channels are the play — Greenport's outer channel, the cut through Sag Harbor, and the deeper edges of Noyack Bay where the bottom drops from six feet to fifteen or better. Drifting bucktails, half-ounce to three-quarter depending on current, tipped with a strip of squid or a white Gulp Swimming Mullet, has been the most consistent producer. The better drifts have come on the outgoing tide, when bait gets pulled out of the shallows and funnels through the deeper cuts — that's when the bigger fluke seem to wake up and feed instead of just holding tight to bottom. Nobody's filling a cooler with jumbos, but a mixed bag with a few keepers in the 18 to 20-inch range is realistic if you put in the drift time and don't get discouraged by the short fish, which there are plenty of.

Striped bass are the interesting story this week, and it lines up with something we flagged last week — that building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would start sharpening the bite at current-driven structure. That's exactly what's happening. With the bay sitting warm through the day, the bass have pushed off the flats and are holding in the deeper holes and current lines, mostly feeding after dark or right around dawn when the water temperature eases off a degree or two. Plum Gut is the obvious spot — the current there never really goes to sleep, and as the tidal range builds toward the new moon, that rip is getting some real push behind it. Same story off Orient Point, where the current line forms hard on a strong ebb. Live eels drifted through the rip, or bunker chunks fished on the bottom in the deeper scour holes, have both worked after sundown. Daytime bass fishing in the open bay has been slow and scattered — not worth grinding through the heat of the afternoon when the fish simply aren't feeding.

Bluefish have been quiet in the Peconic proper, though there's a resurgence building to our west on the Sound's deep reef structure that's worth watching. If that pattern pushes east the way these things sometimes do, Orient Point and the mouth of the bay would be the first places to feel it. I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet, but keep a wire leader in the box just in case.

Weakfish remain a wildcard — a few scattered reports of fish taken incidentally while bottom fishing for porgies, nothing you can build a trip around, but worth a passing cast with a bucktail or soft plastic if you're marking bait on the graph and want to check.

As for water clarity, it's holding up nicely for this time of year, which is good news with bay scallop season prep underway — clean water now means an easier time spotting scallop beds when the season opens. That clarity is also part of why the porgy bite has been so visual and consistent; you can practically watch them working the bottom in the shallower spots.

Looking ahead, the new moon on the 12th should be the thing to watch. Tidal range is going to build noticeably over the next several days, and that means sharper current at every pinch point in the bay — Plum Gut, the Orient rip, the North and South Ferry crossings, the mouth of Three Mile Harbor. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd want the last of the outgoing tide at Plum Gut, right as the light fades, with an eel in the water and patience to match. The porgies aren't going anywhere either — that bite should hold steady as long as this warm, settled weather pattern does.
